benchmark.goal: Which Whisper model should we run with whisper.cpp for podcast transcripts?
benchmark.scope: English speech transcribed offline by whisper.cpp 1.9.6 on one Apple M2 laptop with 8 GB, Metal GPU on, default decoding. Accuracy is word error rate against human transcripts on 24 excerpts of about 100 s from four freely licensed corpora: clean read speech, headset-recorded meetings, the same meetings from a room microphone, and accented earnings calls. Speed is the whole whisper-cli process per minute of audio. Says nothing about other languages, other machines, quantized models, speaker labels, punctuation or timestamps.

reference_suites: Open ASR Leaderboard (Hugging Face, hf-audio/open-asr-leaderboard, built on the ESB benchmark): LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other, AMI, Earnings-22, GigaSpeech, SPGISpeech, TED-LIUM, VoxPopuli. This benchmark uses a subset: LibriSpeech test-clean, AMI (headset and distant mic) and Earnings-22. Omitted: test-other (read speech again, the brief asks for noise, accents and crosstalk), SPGISpeech (licence restricts use), GigaSpeech and Common Voice (gated behind terms of access), TED-LIUM 3 (CC BY-NC-ND), VoxPopuli (not served by the Hugging Face dataset server). No overall score comparable with the leaderboard average is reported.
AMI Meeting Corpus test set, distant-microphone condition, the usual test for far-field and overlapping speech
Earnings-22, built to test recognition of accented English (Del Rio et al., 2022)
standard_metrics: word error rate (WER) after text normalization, with the Whisper English normalizer as on the Open ASR Leaderboard
inverse real-time factor (RTFx: seconds of audio per second of compute); here expressed as seconds of compute per minute of audio
pitfalls: WER depends heavily on normalization (case, punctuation, numbers, fillers like uh/um): the same normalizer is applied to every model and to the references
Whisper can hallucinate or loop on silence, noise and long-form audio; insertions can push WER past 100%, so every output is scored, none dropped

the encoder always processes 30 s windows, so very short clips overstate the cost per minute; excerpts of about 100 s are used and model load is included, which favours smaller models slightly compared with hour-long files
Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of web audio; public test sets such as LibriSpeech (LibriVox audiobooks) may overlap its training data
on Apple Silicon, Metal buffers may not appear in resident set size; the macOS peak memory footprint is used instead
large-v3-turbo has 4 decoder layers instead of 32: release notes report accuracy close to large-v2/v3 for English with a large speed gain, weaker for translation and some languages

nodes.label: Clean audio
nodes.description: Speech recorded close to the speaker: read audiobooks and meetings recorded on headset microphones. The closest case to a podcast interview recorded on good mics.

nodes.label: Poor audio
nodes.description: Speech recorded far from the speaker or over the phone: a room microphone with noise, echo and people talking over each other, and accented speakers on earnings calls.

nodes.label: Read audiobooks
nodes.description: LibriSpeech test-clean (CC BY 4.0): 6 excerpts from 6 speakers, consecutive sentences of one chapter of a LibriVox audiobook.

nodes.label: Meetings, headset mics
nodes.description: AMI Meeting Corpus test set (CC BY 4.0), individual headset microphones: 6 excerpts from 6 meetings, spontaneous conversation, many non-native speakers.

nodes.label: Meetings, room mic
nodes.description: The same 6 AMI excerpts, words and speakers as the headset group, but heard through one far-field room microphone: room noise, echo and crosstalk.

nodes.label: Accented phone calls
nodes.description: Earnings-22 (CC BY-SA 4.0): 6 excerpts of company earnings calls with non-native English speakers, from South Korea, Turkey, Germany, Greece, Russia and Spain, phone or remote audio.

metrics.label: Word error rate
metrics.definition: Per excerpt, (substituted + deleted + inserted words) / reference words, in percent, after the Whisper English text normalizer on both the human transcript and the model output (jiwer 4.0). A failed process is scored on an empty transcript (100%). Averaged over excerpts.

metrics.label: Time per minute of audio
metrics.definition: Wall time of one whisper-cli process transcribing one excerpt, model load included, divided by the excerpt's length in minutes, timed by the measuring script with a monotonic clock

metrics.label: Peak memory
metrics.definition: Peak memory footprint of the whisper-cli process over one excerpt, as reported by macOS /usr/bin/time -l (phys_footprint, which counts Metal GPU buffers in unified memory)
metrics.scope: The whisper-cli process only; it starts no child process

metrics.label: Excerpts transcribed
metrics.definition: Share of excerpts where whisper-cli exited normally and wrote a non-empty transcript

composite.note: Weights record the priorities agreed before measuring (accuracy 0.6, speed 0.3, memory 0.1); no single score is computed

workload.description: 24 excerpts of 94 to 104 s (40 min of audio in all), 6 per source, each a run of consecutive segments of one recording in time order joined by 0.3 s of silence, with the concatenated human transcript as reference. Chosen by scripts/fetch_data.py with a fixed seed before any model was run. Sources: LibriSpeech test-clean (CC BY 4.0, openslr/librispeech_asr rev 71cacbf), AMI Meeting Corpus test set headset and single distant mic (CC BY 4.0, edinburghcstr/ami rev 46f28f2), Earnings-22 (CC BY-SA 4.0, distil-whisper/earnings22 rev 0a034f9; the Hugging Face dataset server indexes only 24 of its 125 calls, none from the African region, so the draw took one call from each of the 5 other non-native regions there and a 6th at random among the remaining non-native calls (a second Asian one)).
workload.usage_pattern: One whisper-cli process per recording, run from the command line on a laptop, as for one podcast episode; here each excerpt stands for one recording

contamination.risk: medium: all four corpora are public and predate Whisper's training (2022); LibriSpeech audio comes from LibriVox, which is on the web. Accuracy may be better than on unpublished podcast audio, for every model

environment.hardware: Apple MacBook, Apple M2 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 10-core GPU), 8 GB unified memory
environment.background: Laptop kept idle during the run (no other application in use; load average about 3 from the window server and the terminal). On battery power (86% at the start), Low Power Mode off, sleep blocked with caffeinate; not on mains as planned.
tools: caffeinate -dims (keeps the Mac awake during the run)

runs.warmup: One untimed 10 s transcription per model before the timed runs, to load the model file into the file cache and compile Metal kernels
runs.order: Excerpts in a shuffled order (seed 7); for each excerpt the order of the five models is shuffled again

artifacts.command: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install jiwer==4.0.0 whisper-normalizer==1.0.1 soundfile certifi && brew install whisper-cpp ffmpeg && ./examples/speech-to-text/scripts/run.sh

limitations: Version 1.1 of the plan. The first full run (v1.0) used whisper-cli's -nt flag for every model; it dropped whole passages of speech (one check: medium on a clean audiobook excerpt, 29.9% WER with -nt against 2.0% without). The flag was removed and every model measured again on the same 24 excerpts; the v1.0 rows are kept in data/runs-v1.0-nt.jsonl and are not compared with these results. Nothing else in the plan changed.

A first run of v1.1 was interrupted when the laptop went to sleep on battery after 14 of 24 excerpts; the rest ran in short wake windows over about 8 hours. With the user's agreement it was set aside for speed and memory and the whole v1.1 measurement was run again with sleep blocked (caffeinate). Its rows are kept in data/runs-v1.1-slept.jsonl. Total measuring time came to about 39 minutes against the 30 planned; the 120 transcripts of the repeat were identical to those of the interrupted run.

One pass per excerpt: decoding is deterministic here. The pilot ran one excerpt per group twice with every model and got identical transcripts, and the final run reproduced the interrupted run's 120 transcripts word for word.
One laptop (M2, 8 GB): on another Mac the speeds change, and the ranking by speed may too; the accuracy figures should carry over to whisper.cpp on other machines.

Excerpts of about 100 s joined from consecutive segments, not continuous hour-long recordings: long-form problems (drift, repetition loops late in a file) are under-tested, and including model load in every excerpt makes the larger models look a little slower per minute than on a full episode.
24 excerpts, 6 per source: the intervals reflect that; one podcast's own audio may differ from all four sources.
English only, multilingual models with language forced to English; the English-only .en variants of tiny to medium, quantized models and full large-v3 were not tested.
Public test sets that may be in Whisper's training data; scores are word errors after normalization, ignoring punctuation, capitalization and speaker labels.
Default decoding settings only; no VAD, prompt or beam-size tuning for any model.
AMI headset and room-mic groups contain the same words from the same meetings, so they are not independent of each other.
Run by Claude for the podcast team, which has no interest in any of the models.

blocks.title: Words each model gets wrong
blocks.description: Poor audio has far more errors for every model, and the spread between excerpts is much wider.

blocks.title: Bigger likely helps on clean audio; poor audio is unclear
blocks.description: On poor audio only {candidate:base} against {candidate:tiny} is clear; one repetition loop by {candidate:turbo} on a room-mic excerpt widens its interval.

blocks.title: Time to transcribe one minute of audio
blocks.description: Model load included, on 100 s excerpts; an hour-long episode spreads the load over more audio.

blocks.title: {candidate:turbo} is likely faster than {candidate:medium}
blocks.description: Above {candidate:base}, each step up is slower than the one below; {candidate:base} and {candidate:tiny} cannot be told apart.
